rationale: B wins because it gives the founder four real doors into the story: P&L, moat strategy, driver experience, and connector infrastructure. A has one strong opener, "Rivian opens 3,500+ fast chargers to rival EVs, betting its network earns more as a utility than a perk," but then spends two angles circling the same premium-pricing fact. B's "Rivian's new stalls will speak both plugs - CCS and NACS on every one" finds a distinct infrastructure beat A left sitting in the fact block like spare parts.
gaps_in_A: "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more than its own" and "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates" are too close. Both ride the same owner-vs-non-owner premium; one should die or be rebuilt around a harder proof point.
A misses the clean connector-standardization angle in "all new stalls will include both CCS and Tesla-style NACS connectors." That is a separate infrastructure story, not just supporting detail.
"the way it has for one walled competitor" smuggles in an outside comparison without naming or proving it. Cute dodge, weak sourcing.
The owner-loyalty angle is soft until Rivian can show retention, usage, or a real price delta. A admits this, but still keeps the angle as if the bones are already there.
gaps_in_B: "The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat" is plausible, but it is not in the supplied facts. This needs a sourced industry comparison before it becomes the spine of a pitch.
"capital-heavy cost center" is an unsupplied characterization. Likely true, but likely true is still not a fact block.

"Every other EV driver just gained 3,500 fast chargers" is a little too sweeping. Access via the Rivian app is real, but compatibility, locations, and connector timing need to be nailed before that headline goes outside.
